title: Galdrastafir: the Icelandic magical staves
family: Not an alphabet. Early modern Icelandic sign-magic: single drawn figures with a named purpose, written in manuscript books of magic (galdrakver, galdraskræður) from about 1500 (AM 434 a 12mo) to the 19th century. They have no sound values. Some contain runes or rune-like strokes. They belong with the charaktêres and the Solomonic seals, not with the runic alphabets.
summary: Galdrastafir are named magical figures ('staves') that Icelandic manuscripts tell the user to carve, draw or carry for a stated purpose, such as protection, victory, finding one's way, winning at wrestling or catching thieves. The oldest known Icelandic manuscript with drawn staves is the medical book AM 434 a 12mo (c. 1500; some date it to the late 15th century). The oldest substantial collection usually cited is the Galdrabók in Stockholm (late 16th to mid-17th century), edited by Natan Lindqvist in 1921. The familiar eight-armed ægishjálmur first appears in Lbs 143 8vo, a Galdrakver of 1670, and the vegvísir in the 19th-century Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to (1847 or 1860, the sources disagree); no stave of this kind is attested from the Viking Age.

firstAttestation.work: AM 434 a 12mo, an Icelandic medical book (lækningabók, 'Lækningakver') with a supplement of galdrastafir on its opening pages; edited by Kristian Kålund as Den islandske lægebog (1907)
firstAttestation.author: Anonymous. The sources differ on the number of hands: one copyist (Gelmir) or two scribes (Vísindavefurinn, answer 81960, as reported in search results).
firstAttestation.date: c. 1500 (Vísindavefurinn 81960 and its English version on why.is, 81995; Gelmir). Other datings found: the second half of the 15th century (a review of Kålund's edition) and the last quarter of the 15th century (Brute Norse). The Hólmavík museum's older web page calls it a 17th-century manuscript, which conflicts with every other source found. Give c. 1500 and note the earlier dating.
firstAttestation.place: Iceland. Now in the Arnamagnæan Collection. Vísindavefurinn (answer 75399) says the book is kept in Copenhagen; the Hólmavík museum's older page says Reykjavík. Not checked against the catalogue.
firstAttestation.locator: The galdrastafir supplement is on the opening pages of the manuscript (why.is 81995). Leaf numbers were not verified. Printed edition: Kålund 1907.
firstAttestation.notes: 'First' here means the oldest surviving manuscript with drawn staves that the sources name, not the first magical sign in Iceland. why.is says only a fragment of the magical booklet survives. Vísindavefurinn (75399) says the manuscript holds an older, four-armed, unnamed stave with the same purpose as the later ægishjálmur, against anger. The Hólmavík museum attributes the wrestling staves Gapaldur and Ginfaxi to it. Roberto Luigi Pagani (Gripla 36, 2025, pp. 241–269) builds his analysis mainly on this and the other earliest grimoires. The Galdrabók remains the oldest substantial collection usually cited: Stockholm, Antikvarisk-topografiska arkivet, ATA Ämb 2 F 16:26 (Gelmir; Smith 2015; English Wikipedia). It has 47 items written by four hands, three Icelanders and a fourth, a Dane working from Icelandic material (English Wikipedia, 'Galdrabók'). Its date: 'from the 1500s' in Lindqvist's 1921 title; c. 1600 in English Wikipedia; late 16th to mid-17th century in Gelmir.

transmission.work: Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, now at the Árni Magnússon Institute, Reykjavík): Fáfnismál, stanzas 16–17; also the prose of Reginsmál
transmission.author: Anonymous
transmission.what: Supplies the NAME, not the sign. In stanza 16 the dragon Fáfnir says he bore the ægishjálmr, the 'helm of terror', over the sons of men while he lay on his treasure; Sigurðr answers in stanza 17. The prose of Reginsmál says all living things feared it. Here it is an object or a terror the dragon wears. No figure is drawn. The early modern stave borrows the name.

transmission.work: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the otter's-ransom story); also Völsunga saga (Fáfnir episode)
transmission.author: Snorri Sturluson (Edda); anonymous (Völsunga saga)
transmission.what: Skáldskaparmál says Fáfnir took a helm that Hreiðmarr had owned and set it on his head, the helm called ægishjálmr, which all living things that see it fear (see quotations; chapter 47 in the text at asatru.is; chapter numbers differ between editions, so cite Faulkes 1998 by page). In Völsunga saga Sigurðr takes the ægishjálmr from the hoard. This is still a helmet in a story, not a drawn stave.

transmission.work: AM 434 a 12mo, an Icelandic medical book with a supplement of staves (ed. Kålund, Den islandske lægebog, 1907)
transmission.author: Anonymous (one or two hands; sources differ)
transmission.what: The oldest surviving Icelandic manuscript with drawn magical staves (Vísindavefurinn 81960; why.is 81995). It includes a four-armed, unnamed stave against anger that Vísindavefurinn treats as an older form of the ægishjálmur. why.is describes it as the oldest Scandinavian grimoire that combines text and drawn signs.

transmission.work: Galdrabók (Stockholm, Antikvarisk-topografiska arkivet, ATA Ämb 2 F 16:26)
transmission.author: Four anonymous scribes: three Icelanders and a Dane working from Icelandic material (English Wikipedia)
transmission.what: The oldest substantial collection: 47 items of spells, many with staves or runes and spoken formulas, in a small parchment booklet of 32 leaves (Gelmir). The formulas call on Christ and Christian powers alongside Óðinn, Þórr and Freyja, and on figures from demonology (Gelmir; Medievalists.net). It shows the stave as a working tool with a stated use. A four-armed helm of awe drawn without crossbars is reported for spell 41 in Flowers's numbering (norse-mythology.org, a popular site; verify in Lindqvist or Flowers).

transmission.date: 1625 – 1683 (a further burning in 1685 was for blasphemy)
transmission.work: Icelandic witch-trial records (the 'burning age', brennuöld)
transmission.author: Alþingi and district courts; documents studied by Ólína Þorvarðardóttir (2000) and others
transmission.what: Owning staves, rune papers and black-art books served as evidence. The first burning was of Jón Rögnvaldsson at Melaeyrar in Svarfaðardalur in 1625, for raising a ghost and owning papers with runic characters (Strandagaldur; English Wikipedia). Strandagaldur gives about 170 accused and 21 burned between 1625 and 1683, only one of them a woman, and lists a 1685 burning for blasphemy outside that span. An article in Scandinavian-Canadian Studies, counting the 71 accused who reached judgment, gives 21 men and one woman burned. The figures depend on which borderline cases are counted; give the range and its sources.

transmission.work: Jón Magnússon, Píslarsaga ('Passion story')
transmission.author: Rev. Jón Magnússon (c. 1610–1696), priest at Eyri in Skutulsfjörður
transmission.what: A first-person account by a priest who believed staves and spells caused his sufferings. He accused a father and son, both named Jón Jónsson, of Kirkjuból in Skutulsfjörður; they were burned in 1656. English Wikipedia gives the date as 10 April 1656; Vísindavefurinn says the first day of summer. It is the fullest contemporary picture of how sorcery was believed to work against a victim. The text survives in one manuscript, in Copenhagen (Bókalind's description of the 1912–14 edition).

transmission.work: Galdrakver, Lbs 143 8vo (National and University Library of Iceland, Reykjavík)
transmission.author: One unknown hand (Gelmir); later owned by Bishop Hannes Finnsson of Skálholt (1739–1796)
transmission.what: A small parchment book of 27 leaves: hymns on the first seven folios, then charms, prayers and galdrastafir with instructions (Gelmir). It holds the oldest example of the ægishjálmur in the eight-armed form known today (Vísindavefurinn 75399; German Wikipedia), with the instruction to make it in lead and imprint it on the forehead when expecting enemies. The leaf is given as 10v (Gelmir) or 11r (Crazy Alchemist); check the manuscript. handrit.is notes that it was published as Galdrakver in 2004.

transmission.work: Galdrabók
transmission.what: The book leaves Iceland. Gelmir says the Swedish scholar Johan Gabriel Sparfwenfeldt acquired it in Copenhagen in 1682. This was not confirmed by a second source.

transmission.work: Rúna- og galdrakver, Lbs 2413 8vo (National and University Library of Iceland)
transmission.author: One copyist (as reported); not named in the sources found
transmission.what: A large collection, reported as 74 leaves with about 200 spells and staves. Popular accounts say it gives nine different ægishjálmar, each to be used 99 times; check that against the manuscript before using it. No individual stave on the page should be attached to it until the handrit.is record or an edition has been read.

transmission.date: 1847 (Strandagaldur) or 1860 (English Wikipedia, 'Vegvísir'; Projekt Forlǫg; Gelmir; runesdb)
transmission.work: The Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to (National and University Library of Iceland, Reykjavík)
transmission.author: Geir Vigfússon (1813–1880), of Akureyri
transmission.what: A 19th-century compilation copied from at least three older manuscripts, one apparently written at Seltjarnarnes about 1810. Its first part holds about 300 alphabets, secret letters and rune rows; its second part has 30 staves with texts (Strandagaldur). It is the first known attestation of the vegvísir, with its name and use, on p. 60 (fol. 27r) (Projekt Forlǫg; English Wikipedia); one account gives fol. 26v.

transmission.work: Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og æfintýri (Leipzig: J. C. Hinrichs, 2 vols)
transmission.author: Jón Árnason (collector)
transmission.what: Vísindavefurinn (75399) says galdrastafir first appear in print in its first volume (1862). It gives the folk tales of sorcerers, the tilberi and its butter, and the powers of staves and black-art books. The section 'Galdramyndir' (in the Wikisource transcription) gives the lead ægishjálmur pressed between the eyebrows, with its verse. Vísindavefurinn says the 1862 volume has no text on the ægishjálmur, so the volume and page of that passage need checking.

transmission.work: Galdrakver, Lbs 2917 a 4to
transmission.author: Olgeir Geirsson (as reported)
transmission.what: A second vegvísir witness, on p. 27, according to Tomáš Vlasatý (Projekt Forlǫg) as reported by English Wikipedia and other accounts. Not checked against the manuscript.

transmission.work: Galdrakver, Lbs 4627 8vo
transmission.author: Unknown; one account says three unidentified scribes; written in the Eyjafjörður area (Projekt Forlǫg)
transmission.what: A third vegvísir witness, visibly different from the Huld figure and given with a Christian instruction (Projekt Forlǫg; The Witch Index). Not checked against the manuscript.

transmission.work: An article by Ólafur Davíðsson on Icelandic magical signs and books (exact title, journal and pages not verified)
transmission.author: Ólafur Davíðsson (1862–1903)
transmission.what: Projekt Forlǫg names it as the first publication of the vegvísir. Justin Foster says it was based on drawings made for the author, and that Flowers's Huld material derives from it, at several removes.

transmission.work: En isländsk svartkonstbok från 1500-talet (Uppsala: Appelbergs boktryckeri aktiebolag)
transmission.author: Natan Lindqvist (ed. and Swedish trans.)
transmission.what: The first edition of the Galdrabók: a diplomatic edition with a Swedish translation. How it reproduces the staves was not checked.

transmission.date: 1940–1943 (also given as 1941–1943; posthumous, Ólafur died in 1903)
transmission.work: Galdur og galdramál á Íslandi (Reykjavík: Sögufélag)
transmission.author: Ólafur Davíðsson
transmission.what: The great Icelandic-language survey of magic and sorcery cases, cited throughout Vísindavefurinn's answers on Icelandic witchcraft. That it reproduces many staves with their uses is the compiler's statement and was not checked.

transmission.date: 1989; second, revised edition (dates disagree, see sources)
transmission.work: The Galdrabók: An Icelandic Grimoire (York Beach, ME: Samuel Weiser, 1989); 2nd revised ed. as The Galdrabók: An Icelandic Book of Magic (Smithville, TX: Rûna-Raven Press; later Lodestar)
transmission.author: Stephen E. Flowers (ed. and English trans.)
transmission.what: The standard English translation of the Galdrabók. Its Appendix A, 'Other Icelandic Sources', adds material from the Huld manuscript, the Kreddur manuscript, Svend Grundtvig's collection, Jón Árnason's collection and manuscripts collected by Ólafur Davíðsson. Projekt Forlǫg says the vegvísir appears in the 1989 book only in a note on p. 88, and that this note started the belief that it is in the Galdrabók. That Flowers keeps Lindqvist's numbering is not verified.

transmission.work: Galdrar á Íslandi: Íslensk galdrabók (Reykjavík: Almenna bókafélagið; series Íslensk þjóðfræði; 466 pp.)
transmission.author: Matthías Viðar Sæmundsson (ed.)
transmission.what: An Icelandic edition and study of Icelandic magical texts and staves, reviewed in Saga (1993) as a work built on primary sources.

transmission.work: Strandagaldur: the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery and Witchcraft, Hólmavík (first part opened in 2000); Ólína Þorvarðardóttir, Brennuöldin (2000)
transmission.author: Strandagaldur (Magnús Rafnsson and others); Ólína Þorvarðardóttir
transmission.what: Displays and booklets that present the staves to a wide public, and a doctoral study of the trial documents and their folklore. Many images now circulating online derive from redrawn reproductions rather than fresh tracings of the manuscripts.

transmission.work: Icelandic Magic: Aims, Tools and Techniques of the Icelandic Sorcerers (Avalonia)
transmission.author: Christopher Alan Smith
transmission.what: A study organised by the aims of the spells, drawing on six Icelandic manuscripts dated 1500 to 1860 (publisher's description).

transmission.work: 'The Mediterranean origin …' (title as shown in search), Gripla 36 (2025), 241–269
transmission.author: Roberto Luigi Pagani
transmission.what: Argues that the galdrastafir adapt esoteric motifs from the Mediterranean, probably from the late Middle Ages between Greece and Italy, working mainly from the earliest grimoires, including AM 434 a 12mo. This is one scholar's argument; report it as such.

transmission.work: Popular reception (tattoos, jewellery, souvenirs, games, modern heathen imagery)
transmission.what: The vegvísir and the ægishjálmur become popular emblems and are often mislabelled as 'Viking' symbols or a 'Viking compass'. Many commercial designs are new and have no manuscript source.

claims.claim: The galdrastafir are Viking-Age or ancient Norse symbols.
claims.evidence: No stave of the later manuscript type is known from runic inscriptions or Viking-Age objects. The oldest drawn staves are in AM 434 a 12mo (c. 1500); the Galdrabók follows (late 16th–17th century). The eight-armed ægishjálmur first appears in Lbs 143 8vo (1670) and the vegvísir in the 19th-century Huld manuscript (ÍB 383 4to).

claims.claim: The vegvísir is a 'Viking compass' or 'runic compass'.
claims.evidence: This is a modern label. The Huld caption makes it a stave to carry so as not to lose one's way in snowstorms and bad weather. It has no navigational use and no Viking-Age attestation; its known witnesses are all 19th-century.
sources: Projekt Forlǫg (Tomáš Vlasatý), 'Origins of the vegvísir symbol'

claims.claim: The vegvísir appears in the Galdrabók.
claims.evidence: Rejected by the sources checked. Vlasatý (Projekt Forlǫg) calls it a common mistake that began in the late 1980s, when Flowers printed the vegvísir in a note on p. 88 of his 1989 Galdrabók. The known witnesses are the Huld manuscript (ÍB 383 4to), Lbs 2917 a 4to and Lbs 4627 8vo, all 19th-century. Lindqvist's edition itself was not consulted, so state the negative as the finding of these sources.

claims.claim: The Huld manuscript (ÍB 383 4to) was compiled by Geir Vigfússon in 1847.
claims.evidence: The compiler, Geir Vigfússon (1813–1880) of Akureyri, is agreed. The date is not: 1847 (Strandagaldur, galdrasyning.is) against 1860 (English Wikipedia 'Vegvísir'; Projekt Forlǫg; Gelmir; runesdb). The handrit.is record could not be read. Give both.

claims.claim: The oldest eight-armed ægishjálmur is in Lbs 143 8vo.
claims.evidence: Vísindavefurinn (75399) says the oldest example of the eight-armed form known today is in the parchment manuscript Lbs 143 8vo (about the mid-17th century; handrit.is: 1670), and that an older, four-armed, unnamed stave with the same purpose is in a medical book in Copenhagen (AM 434 a 12mo). The leaf is given as 10v or 11r.
sources: handrit.is record for Lbs 143 8vo (title and date as shown in search)

claims.claim: The Galdrabók dates from the 16th century.
claims.evidence: Lindqvist's title says 'from the 1500s'. English Wikipedia dates it to c. 1600, with four hands working from perhaps the late 16th century into the mid-17th; Gelmir gives the late 16th to mid-17th century. Report both.

claims.claim: The ægishjálmur stave is the 'helm of terror' that Fáfnir wears in the Edda.
claims.evidence: The NAME is documented in Fáfnismál 16–17, the prose of Reginsmál, Snorri's Skáldskaparmál and Völsunga saga, where the ægishjálmr is a helm or a terror that the dragon wears. No figure is drawn or described there. The drawn stave is early modern. Whether the stave preserves an older idea or simply borrows a famous name is a matter of interpretation.

claims.claim: The 'ægis-' of ægishjálmur refers to the sea-giant Ægir.
claims.evidence: Cleasby–Vigfússon gloss ægis-hjálmr as 'a helmet of terror' and, under hjálmr, compare the Greek aegis, not the sea-giant. English Wikipedia ('Helm of Awe') derives the first element from œgir, 'one who frightens', from agi, 'awe, terror'. Some popular sources link it to the sea-giant Ægir; the sources checked do not.

claims.claim: Staves were used as evidence in the Icelandic witch trials of 1625 to 1683.
claims.evidence: The trial records and the Píslarsaga name staves, rune papers and black-art books as evidence. The first burning, of Jón Rögnvaldsson, was in 1625, for raising a ghost and owning papers with runic characters. Strandagaldur gives 21 burned between 1625 and 1683, one of them a woman; a Scandinavian-Canadian Studies article gives 21 men and one woman among the 71 who reached judgment. Strandagaldur says about a third of the trials turn on owning grimoires or staves (as reported in a review of Angurgapi).
sources: Strandagaldur, 'The Witch-hunts in Iceland' and 'The Executed'

claims.evidence: Some writers (notably Flowers) stress runic elements and bind-rune construction. Others stress continental learned magic. Vlasatý (Projekt Forlǫg) argues the vegvísir borrows from the continental 'Solomon' tradition, and Pagani (Gripla 2025) argues that the staves adapt Mediterranean esoteric motifs, working from the earliest grimoires. The staves themselves mix runes, Latin letters and non-letter strokes. No single origin is shown.

claims.claim: Each stave named in the manuscripts has one fixed shape.
claims.evidence: The same name is given to different figures in different manuscripts. The ægishjálmur alone appears as a four-armed unnamed stave (AM 434 a 12mo), a four-armed helm without crossbars (Galdrabók, as reported), the eight-armed form (Lbs 143 8vo) and nine different helms (Lbs 2413 8vo, as reported). The Lbs 4627 8vo vegvísir differs visibly from the Huld one. The modern 'standard' shapes are selections, often redrawn and tidied.

letters.name: Ægishjálmur ('helm of awe', 'helm of terror')
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: protection against enemies and their anger. Lbs 143 8vo: it is to be made in lead, and a man who expects to meet his enemies imprints it on his forehead (English rendering reproduced on Wikimedia Commons). Jón Árnason's collection ('Galdramyndir'): shaped in lead and pressed onto the forehead between the eyebrows, with the verse given under quotations; whoever went against an enemy with it was sure of victory, and a second verse protects against the anger of chieftains.
letters.form: The name covers many figures: a four-armed unnamed form (AM 434 a 12mo), a four-armed form reported for the Galdrabók, and the eight-armed form first found in Lbs 143 8vo (1670). What follows is the eight-armed form that modern reproductions treat as standard. It is NOT a tracing of a named manuscript page, and the proportions given are the compiler's estimates, not measurements. (1) A small circle at the centre. Some versions use a dot or leave the centre open where the arms meet. (2) Eight equal straight arms run out from the rim of the circle at 45° intervals: up, down, left, right and the four diagonals. (3) All eight arms are alike, so the figure has eightfold symmetry. Each arm ends in a three-pronged fork like a trident (Ψ). The middle prong continues the arm in a straight line; the two side prongs rise from the ends of a short crossbar set at right angles to the arm. (4) Many renderings also cross each shaft with one or more short bars at right angles, between the central circle and the fork. The number varies between reproductions. (5) The compiler describes no ring-ends; whether the manuscript form has any must be checked. All strokes are of even weight.
letters.note: Judged consistent with the standard published eight-armed form: eight identical trident-ended arms around a centre, with crossbars on the shafts. The details are not sourced: the size of the centre, the length and angle of the side prongs, the number and place of the crossbars, and whether any ends carry small circles. Trace them from Lbs 143 8vo, fol. 10v or 11r (sources differ; handrit.is appears to hold images), and print that source under the drawing. Do NOT trace from the Galdrabók for this form, because its helm is reported as four-armed. The name comes from Fáfnir's helm in the Edda; the stave is early modern.

letters.name: Vegvísir ('way-shower', 'signpost')
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: according to the Huld caption, a man who carries these staves will not lose his way in snowstorms or bad weather, even when the way is unknown to him.
letters.form: Overall plan only: (1) a small central circle; (2) eight straight arms running out from it at 45° intervals, like the ægishjálmur; (3) unlike the ægishjálmur, each of the eight arms ends differently, so the figure has NO rotational symmetry. The arm-ends are drawn from a small repertoire: three-pronged forks (trident ends), two-pronged forks, short crossbars across the shaft, and small ring-ends (circles) at the tips of some prongs or shafts. The compiler cannot say, arm by arm, which end sits on which arm in ÍB 383 4to. DO NOT DRAW IT FROM THIS DESCRIPTION. Trace it from the manuscript image (ÍB 383 4to, p. 60 / fol. 27r) or a named printed reproduction. Many modern designs enclose the figure in a ring, often with runes around it. The compiler believes the Huld figure has no such ring; verify.
letters.note: The overall plan is consistent with the published Huld figure as generally reproduced, but the arm-by-arm detail is missing, so the confidence stays low. First known attestation: the Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to (NOT Lbs 143 8vo), p. 60 (fol. 27r; one account gives 26v), 1847 or 1860. Later witnesses, as reported by Vlasatý: Lbs 2917 a 4to (Olgeir Geirsson, 1868–69, p. 27) and Lbs 4627 8vo (19th century), whose figure is visibly different; caption the drawing with the one traced. Its fame is modern: tattoos, jewellery, souvenirs, 'Viking' merchandise.

letters.name: Gapaldur
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: victory in glíma (Icelandic wrestling). It is used as a pair with Ginfaxi, kept in the shoes: Gapaldur under the heel of the right foot, Ginfaxi under the toes of the left foot (English Wikipedia list of staves; the Hólmavík museum's older page).
letters.form: Not reliably known to the compiler. No description is given, so that a wrong drawing is not presented as the manuscript's. Trace it from a source reproduction and record the manuscript shelfmark it cites.
letters.note: One of the 'glímustafir' (wrestling staves). The Hólmavík museum's older page attributes the pair to AM 434 a 12mo, but it also calls that manuscript 17th-century and places it in Reykjavík, both of which conflict with other sources. Confirm in Kålund 1907 before captioning.

letters.name: Ginfaxi
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: victory in glíma, used with Gapaldur, under the toes of the left foot (English Wikipedia list of staves; the Hólmavík museum's older page).
letters.form: Not reliably known to the compiler. No description is given. Trace it from the same reproduction used for Gapaldur so that the pair matches.
letters.note: Shown as a pair with Gapaldur. Manuscript source reported as AM 434 a 12mo by the Hólmavík museum only; confirm.

letters.name: Þjófastafur ('thief-stave')
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: to reveal a thief, or to force a thief to return what was stolen. The procedure differs from manuscript to manuscript and is not given here.
letters.form: Not one form. The name is given to several different staves in different manuscripts. No description is given. Choose one manuscript version, trace it, and caption it with that shelfmark.
letters.note: Thief-catching spells are among the aims attested for the Galdrabók (Medievalists.net) and are also a continental charm genre. The shared aim does not prove borrowing. No manuscript source for a particular þjófastafur was confirmed in this check.

letters.name: Smjörhnútur ('butter-knot')
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: a test for 'tilberi butter'. Strandagaldur says the sign is carved into the butter, and if it is tilberi butter it crumbles like foam or bursts into pieces. In the folklore printed by Jón Árnason, the test is a cross drawn in the butter with a finger. The tilberi is a creature a woman makes to steal milk.
letters.form: Not reliably known to the compiler. No description is given. Trace it from a named reproduction.
letters.note: Optional for the page. The tilberi lore is in Jón Árnason's collection (1862–64); the sign's manuscript source was not identified in this check.

letters.name: Hulinhjálmur / Huliðshjálmur ('helm of concealment')
letters.value: Purpose, not a letter: invisibility. Several different figures carry the name.
letters.translit: hulinhjálmur, huliðshjálmur (Old Norse huliðshjálmr; Cleasby–Vigfússon give hulins-hjálmr as a less correct form)
letters.form: Not one form, and not reliably known to the compiler. No description is given. Trace a named manuscript version.
letters.note: Optional for the page. Like the ægishjálmur, the name is older than any drawn stave: Cleasby–Vigfússon list huliðs-hjálmr, 'a hidden helm'. The Old Norse passages were not identified in this check.

lettersSource: These are staves, not letters: each entry is one named figure the page will show. 'value' holds the stated purpose, 'translit' the name and its gloss, and numeric is always null. No form was traced from a manuscript image, because images could not be downloaded or pages fetched. The ægishjálmur description follows the eight-armed form standard in modern reproductions (medium confidence for the scheme, not for the proportions). The vegvísir gives only the overall plan (low). The others are left blank on purpose (low). Before drawing, trace each stave from ONE named source: Lbs 143 8vo (fol. 10v or 11r) for the eight-armed ægishjálmur; the Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to, p. 60 (fol. 27r), for the vegvísir; AM 434 a 12mo (Kålund 1907) for Gapaldur and Ginfaxi if that attribution is confirmed; otherwise Flowers or Ólafur Davíðsson, naming the manuscript they cite. Print that source under the drawing.

uses.use: A stated aim for each stave
uses.evidence: The manuscripts give each stave a purpose: for example protection, victory over enemies, calming anger, catching thieves, protecting a horse, wrestling, and finding one's way. Smith's study is organised around these 'aims'. The list is a general one; item-by-item attributions are to be verified in Lindqvist and Flowers.

The instructions say to carve the stave, draw it, cast or press it in lead, or carry it on the body or in a shoe, often with a spoken formula. Examples: the ægishjálmur made in lead and imprinted on the forehead (Lbs 143 8vo; Jón Árnason); an unnamed stave against anger drawn on the forehead (AM 434 a 12mo, as reported by Brute Norse: with yarrow soaked in blood; not verified); the wrestling staves in the shoes; the vegvísir carried.

The Galdrabók's spoken formulas call on Christ and Christian powers together with Óðinn, Þórr, Freyja and other Norse figures, and on figures from demonology (Gelmir; Medievalists.net). why.is says the spells of AM 434 a 12mo mix Christian prayers with Hebrew divine names.
In the witch trials of 1625 to 1683, owning staves or black-art books was evidence against the accused (Ólína Þorvarðardóttir 2000; Strandagaldur; Píslarsaga, 1656 case).

Since the late 20th century the staves have been used as emblems: tattoos, jewellery, Icelandic souvenirs, museum displays (Strandagaldur, from 2000), games and modern heathen imagery. Many designs sold as galdrastafir have no manuscript source.

quotations.text: Beri maður stafi þessa á sér villist maður ekki í hríðum né vondu veðri þó ókunnugur sé.
quotations.translation: Original (caption of the vegvísir) as reproduced in English Wikipedia and other accounts; some reproductions end 'ókunnugur sá'. Not checked against the manuscript image. Compiler's own paraphrase: 'If a man carries these staves on him, he will not lose his way in snowstorms or bad weather, even when the way is unknown to him.'
quotations.source: Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to (Geir Vigfússon; 1847 or 1860), p. 60 (fol. 27r), caption to the vegvísir

quotations.text: Ægishjálm er ég ber / milli brúna mér
quotations.translation: Original (modern Icelandic spelling) as printed in the Wikisource transcription of Jón Árnason's collection. Compiler's own paraphrase: 'I bear the helm of awe between my brows.' It is spoken while pressing a lead ægishjálmur onto the forehead between the eyebrows.
quotations.source: Jón Árnason, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og æfintýri (Leipzig, 1862–64), 'Galdrasögur: Galdramyndir'. Justin Foster cites p. 452 of the 1862 volume; Vísindavefurinn (75399) says the 1862 volume has no text on the ægishjálmur. Check the volume and page before citing a page.

quotations.text: Ægishjálm bar ek / of alda sonum, / meðan ek of menjum lák
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse (Fáfnir speaking), in a normalised spelling found in modern online texts; the Codex Regius reads 'vm alda sonom', and editions differ ('of', 'um'). Neckel–Kuhn print it in their own orthography. Compiler's own paraphrase: 'I wore the helm of terror over the sons of men while I lay upon the treasures.'
quotations.source: Fáfnismál, stanza 16, lines 1–3; Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to), ed. Neckel–Kuhn 1983. The stanza number 16 agrees across the editions found (skaldic.org; Open Book Publishers).

quotations.text: Fáfnir hafði þá tekit hjálm, er Hreiðmarr hafði átt, ok setti á höfuð sér, er kallaðr var ægishjálmr, er öll kvikvendi hræðast, er sjá
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse, normalised, as given in the text at asatru.is. Compiler's own paraphrase: 'Fáfnir had then taken a helm that Hreiðmarr had owned and set it on his head; it was called the ægishjálmr, which all living things that see it fear.'
quotations.source: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, the otter's-ransom story (chapter 47 in the asatru.is text; cite Faulkes 1998 by page)

links.relation: Overlap and contrast. Staves sometimes include runes or rune-like strokes, and Icelandic magical manuscripts often also copy rune rows and cipher alphabets; the Huld manuscript holds about 300 alphabets. The staves themselves are not runes, have no sound values and are not Viking Age.

Like the charaktêres, these are signs that stand for no sounds, drawn for a named magical aim. Pagani (Gripla 2025) argues for descent from Mediterranean esoteric motifs; this is argued, not shown stave by stave.

Continental parallel: Solomonic and planetary seals and characters circulated in Danish and Norwegian 'black books' (svartebøker) and their sources. Vlasatý links the vegvísir to the 'Solomon' tradition. Their influence on Icelandic staves is argued, not demonstrated stave by stave.
why.is says the spells of AM 434 a 12mo, the oldest manuscript with staves, mix Christian prayers with Hebrew divine names. Check the specific items before quoting.
The Icelandic charm books mix Icelandic with Latin and garbled Latin or divine-name formulas, a sign of contact with continental learned charms. Check the specific items before quoting.

cautions: This file was fact-checked by web search only. Page fetching was unavailable and images could not be viewed, so many points rest on search-result snippets and summaries of the named pages. Neither the handrit.is records nor Lindqvist, Flowers or Kålund were read directly.

Shelfmark trap, which the first draft of this file fell into: the Huld manuscript is ÍB 383 4to (19th century). Lbs 143 8vo is a different book, the Galdrakver of 1670, with the oldest eight-armed ægishjálmur. Do not mix them up.

Do not draw the vegvísir, Gapaldur, Ginfaxi, Þjófastafur, Smjörhnútur or Hulinhjálmur from this file. Their forms were not available with enough certainty. Trace each from one named source and print the source under the drawing. Even the ægishjálmur description is a generic modern form, not a manuscript tracing.

Dates in dispute: the Huld manuscript, 1847 against 1860; the Galdrabók, '1500s' (Lindqvist's title) against c. 1600 to the mid-17th century; AM 434 a 12mo, late 15th century against c. 1500; the 1656 burning, 10 April against the first day of summer. Give both until the sources are checked.
Do not call any stave Viking Age or 'ancient'. Report 'Viking compass' and similar labels only as modern labels, with a date range.

Name traps: Geir Vigfússon (1813–1880, compiler of Huld) is not Guðbrandur Vigfússon (1827–1889, the lexicographer of Cleasby–Vigfússon). The Huld manuscript is not the folklore periodical Huld (Reykjavík, 1890s, recalled; not verified). The ægis- of ægishjálmur is not the sea-giant Ægir in the dictionaries checked.

One name does not mean one shape. Ægishjálmur, þjófastafur and hulinhjálmur are each given to several different figures, and the vegvísir differs between manuscripts. Caption every drawing with the manuscript or edition it follows.

Much of what circulates online, including many 'galdrastafir' sold on jewellery and shown on souvenir sites, is redrawn, simplified or newly invented. Justin Foster notes that Flowers's Huld material comes at several removes from the manuscript. Accept a stave only with a manuscript shelfmark or a scholarly edition behind it.

Stephen E. Flowers is a trained runologist (PhD) and also, under the name Edred Thorsson, a founder of a living esoteric order (the Rune-Gild). Cite his editions for the text. Do not reproduce the emblems or texts of living organisations, including modern heathen bodies that use the staves.
The witch trials concern real people who were executed. Report them from the records, without sensationalism, and do not present the staves as effective or as fraudulent.

To the compiler's knowledge, the vegvísir and the ægishjálmur are not catalogued as hate symbols. Even so, keep them in their manuscript context and do not set them beside the runes that are (see the runes item's cautions).

confidence: SOLID: the staves are early modern, not Viking Age. The oldest surviving manuscript with drawn staves is AM 434 a 12mo (c. 1500 or late 15th century; Vísindavefurinn). The Galdrabók (Stockholm, ATA Ämb 2 F 16:26; four hands) is the oldest substantial collection, edited by Lindqvist (Uppsala, 1921) and translated by Flowers (Weiser, 1989). The eight-armed ægishjálmur first appears in Lbs 143 8vo (Galdrakver, 1670). The vegvísir's first known attestation is the Huld manuscript, ÍB 383 4to, compiled by Geir Vigfússon (1813–1880) of Akureyri, p. 60; its caption ('Beri maður stafi þessa á sér …') makes it a stave against losing one's way in storms. The name ægishjálmr comes from Fáfnir's helm in Fáfnismál 16, Reginsmál, Skáldskaparmál and Völsunga saga, where it is not a drawn sign. The witch trials ran from 1625 (Jón Rögnvaldsson) to 1683, with 21 or 22 burnings and only one woman, and include the 1656 Kirkjuból case behind the Píslarsaga. Gapaldur goes under the right heel and Ginfaxi under the left toes. The verse 'Ægishjálm er ég ber / milli brúna mér' is printed in Jón Árnason's collection. SHAKY: the Huld date (1847 or 1860); folio numbers (vegvísir 27r or 26v; Lbs 143 8vo ægishjálmur 10v or 11r); the volume and page of the Jón Árnason ægishjálmur passage; the date, hands and repository of AM 434 a 12mo; the Galdrabók's provenance (Sparfwenfeldt, 1682, single source); the date of Flowers's second edition; whether Flowers keeps Lindqvist's numbering; the 1656 burning date; the manuscript sources of Gapaldur, Ginfaxi, Smjörhnútur, Þjófastafur and Hulinhjálmur; the Lbs 2413 8vo contents; the Angurgapi date; the title of Ólafur Davíðsson's 1903 article. FORMS: the ægishjálmur is given at medium confidence for its general scheme only. The vegvísir has only its overall plan (low). The other five are deliberately left undescribed (low) and must be traced from a named source.

corrections: Huld manuscript shelfmark corrected from Lbs 143 8vo to ÍB 383 4to (Strandagaldur 'Galdraskræður'; Projekt Forlǫg; English Wikipedia 'Vegvísir'; runesdb). Lbs 143 8vo is a different manuscript, the Galdrakver of 1670. Fixed throughout: summary, transmission, claims, letters, quotations, sources.

First attestation moved from the Galdrabók to AM 434 a 12mo (c. 1500; late 15th century in some sources), which Vísindavefurinn (81960) and why.is (81995) name as the oldest Icelandic manuscript with galdrastafir. The Galdrabók is kept as the oldest substantial collection.
Summary corrected: the eight-armed ægishjálmur first appears in Lbs 143 8vo (1670, 17th century), not in a 19th-century Huld manuscript (Vísindavefurinn 75399; German Wikipedia).

Vegvísir caption corrected from 'Beri maður staf þennan' (singular) to 'Beri maður stafi þessa' ('these staves', plural), as reproduced in the sources; variant ending 'sá' noted; locator added as p. 60 (fol. 27r), with 26v as a variant.

Ægishjálm verse ('Ægishjálm er ég ber / milli brúna mér'): its source corrected from 'Flowers 1989 / an unverified manuscript, possibly the Galdrabók' to Jón Árnason, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og æfintýri, 'Galdramyndir' (Wikisource transcription; norse-mythology.org; Foster cites p. 452). The wording is confirmed.

Galdrabók repository corrected from 'library of Vitterhetsakademien, no shelfmark' to Antikvarisk-topografiska arkivet, Stockholm, ATA Ämb 2 F 16:26 (Gelmir; Smith 2015; English Wikipedia); 32 parchment leaves (Gelmir).
Galdrabók fourth hand: 'may be Danish' changed to 'a Dane working from Icelandic material' (English Wikipedia).

Witch-trial figures: 'about two dozen, end 1683 or 1685' replaced by 21 burned 1625–1683 with one woman, of about 170 accused (Strandagaldur), or 21 men and one woman among the 71 who reached judgment (Scandinavian-Canadian Studies article); the 1685 burning was for blasphemy (Strandagaldur list).
Jón Rögnvaldsson (1625): place (Melaeyrar, Svarfaðardalur) and charges (raising a ghost; papers with runic characters) added from Strandagaldur and English Wikipedia.

Píslarsaga: the 1656 burning dated 10 April (English Wikipedia) or the first day of summer (Vísindavefurinn); Jón Magnússon's dates (c. 1610–1696) added; editions corrected: Sigfús Blöndal, Copenhagen: Hið íslenska fræðafélag, 1912–1914 (also 1913 or 1914), Sigurður Nordal 1967, Matthías Viðar Sæmundsson, Mál og menning, 2001.
Lbs 2413 8vo: date added as 1780–1820 (handrit.is title listing) or about 1800; reported contents (74 leaves, about 200 spells, nine ægishjálmar) added as secondary.

Vegvísir witnesses: Lbs 4627 8vo confirmed (no longer 'recalled without confidence'), and Lbs 2917 a 4to (Olgeir Geirsson, 1868–69, p. 27) added, both after Vlasatý as reported by English Wikipedia and Projekt Forlǫg.
Claim 'the vegvísir appears in the Galdrabók': the evidence is now the sources' rejection of it. Vlasatý traces the error to a note on p. 88 of Flowers 1989.

Flowers editions: the second edition's date is given as reported in each source (WorldCat ©2005; Google Books and booksellers 2011, Lodestar; English Wikipedia 'Galdrabók' 1995), not as a single 2005. Appendix A contents confirmed (Huld, Kreddur, Grundtvig, Jón Árnason, Ólafur Davíðsson).
Ólafur Davíðsson, Galdur og galdramál: '1940–1943' kept with the variant 1941–1943; the series number 'Sögurit 20' removed (not found).
Lindqvist 1921: publisher confirmed as Appelbergs boktryckeri aktiebolag, Uppsala; the unverified claim of a 'facsimile-based reproduction of the staves' removed.
Matthías Viðar Sæmundsson 1992: confirmed (Almenna bókafélagið; Íslensk þjóðfræði; 466 pp.; ISBN 9979400684); 'verify' removed.
Ólína Þorvarðardóttir 2000: confirmed (Háskólaútgáfan; doctoral thesis); 2nd edition 2023 added.
Smith, Icelandic Magic: date confirmed as 2015 (Avalonia); the alternative '2016' and the unverified place removed.
Kålund 1907: confirmed, with series (KDVS Skrifter, 6. Række) and printer (B. Lunos).

Cleasby–Vigfússon: the headword is huliðs-hjálmr (hulins-hjálmr is given as less correct), not hulins-hjálmr; ægis-hjálmr is glossed 'a helmet of terror', compared with Greek aegis under hjálmr (3). Hulinhjálmur translit and the ægis-/Ægir claim updated.
Skáldskaparmál passage on the ægishjálmr located (chapter 47 in the asatru.is text) and added as a quotation in the original with the compiler's paraphrase.
Fáfnismál 16: the stanza number is confirmed, and the note on spelling now records the Codex Regius reading 'vm alda sonom' and the variants 'of'/'um'.

Huld contents and compiler: Geir Vigfússon's dates (1813–1880), about 300 alphabets, 30 staves with texts, and at least three model manuscripts added (Strandagaldur; Projekt Forlǫg). The unverified statement that Huld 'gives forms of the ægishjálmur' removed.

Gapaldur/Ginfaxi: the foot placement is confirmed (English Wikipedia list; Hólmavík museum page); the 'verify, may be swapped' hedge was removed; the manuscript attribution to AM 434 a 12mo (museum page only) was added, with its conflicts.
Strandagaldur museum: opening in 2000 confirmed.

New transmission entries added: Lbs 143 8vo (1670), Galdrabók provenance (Sparfwenfeldt, 1682, single source), Lbs 2917 a 4to, Lbs 4627 8vo, Ólafur Davíðsson's 1903 article (first print of the vegvísir), Smith 2015, Pagani 2025.
ægishjálmur note corrected: do not trace the eight-armed form from the Galdrabók, whose helm is reported as four-armed (norse-mythology.org); trace from Lbs 143 8vo.

URLs: the two bare 'https://handrit.is/' entries and 'https://www.galdrasyning.is/' were removed and replaced with URLs seen in search results (the handrit.is Lbs 143 8vo record, the handrit.is title listing, galdrasyning.is pages). No unseen URL was added.
unresolved: Huld manuscript date: 1847 (Strandagaldur) or 1860 (English Wikipedia, Projekt Forlǫg, Gelmir). The handrit.is record for ÍB 383 4to could not be read.
Vegvísir leaf in ÍB 383 4to: p. 60 / fol. 27r, or fol. 26v.

AM 434 a 12mo: date (second half or last quarter of the 15th century, c. 1500, early 16th century), number of hands (one or two), and repository (Copenhagen per Vísindavefurinn; Reykjavík per the Hólmavík page).

Jón Árnason's ægishjálmur passage: Foster cites p. 452 of the 1862 volume and Wikisource prints it under 'Galdramyndir', but Vísindavefurinn says the 1862 volume has no text on the ægishjálmur. The volume, page and printing are unresolved.

Galdrabók: the shelfmark rests on Gelmir and Smith, not the repository catalogue; the provenance (Sparfwenfeldt, Copenhagen, 1682) has a single source; the four-armed helm in 'spell 41' rests on a popular site.
Flowers's second edition: 1995 (English Wikipedia 'Galdrabók'), ©2005 (WorldCat) or 2011 (Google Books; Lodestar). Whether Flowers keeps Lindqvist's 47-item numbering was not verified.
1656 Kirkjuból burning: 10 April (English Wikipedia) or the first day of summer (Vísindavefurinn).
Total burnings: 21 (Strandagaldur) or 22 (Scandinavian-Canadian Studies article, 21 men and one woman). The author of the article was not identified.
Magnús Rafnsson, Angurgapi: date of publication (2003 in the draft) not found.
Ólafur Davíðsson's 1903 article: title, journal and pages not found. Galdur og galdramál: 1940 or 1941 as the first year.
Manuscript sources of Gapaldur and Ginfaxi (AM 434 a 12mo, museum page only), and of Smjörhnútur, Þjófastafur and Hulinhjálmur (not identified).
Lbs 2413 8vo contents (74 leaves, about 200 spells, nine ægishjálmar) rest on popular sites.

Forms: no stave was traced from an image. The ægishjálmur proportions and crossbar count, and the vegvísir arm-ends and the absence of an enclosing ring in Huld, are unverified. Five staves have no form.
The folklore periodical Huld (Reykjavík, 1890s) was not verified.
Pagani 2025: the full article title was not seen.
